title: Sarees, Trolls, and the Croisette: What India's Cannes 2026 Moment Really Says About Us
excerpt: Diana Penty's gold Manish Malhotra drape and Huma Qureshi's Banarasi weave earned global applause. Then Alia Bhatt's viral red-carpet clip turned the festival into a mirror for the diaspora's complicated relationship with its own stars.
body:
The 79th Cannes Film Festival, running May 12 to 23, has become an annual referendum on Indian soft power — and this year, the verdict is split. On one side of the Croisette, Indian designers are having a banner year. On the other, Indian social media is doing what it does best: tearing down the people it should be celebrating.

## The Fashion That Stopped the Carpet

Diana Penty arrived at the Bharat Pavilion in a custom Manish Malhotra creation that was part heritage artefact, part couture statement: a gold knitted shimmer saree with a sculptural blouse and metallic accessories, priced at ₹1.95 lakh and handcrafted to showcase traditional Indian textile techniques on a global platform. This is her third consecutive Cannes appearance as a BMW India ambassador, and she has graduated from "Bollywood actress at a film festival" to something closer to "cultural representative."

Hours later, Penty reappeared on the main red carpet in a custom Amit Aggarwal gown — a futuristic, ruby-red number built around an engineered Ikat weave, with black accents that turned a traditional Indian textile into something that looked beamed in from a science-fiction runway. The dual looks — one reverential, one radically modern — captured exactly the kind of range that Indian fashion has been reaching for on the world stage.

She was not alone. Huma Qureshi chose a purple-and-gold Banarasi saree from Shanti Banaras, featuring handwoven brocade and palm-tree motifs that nodded to the Riviera setting while anchoring the look firmly in Varanasi's weaving tradition. Aditi Rao Hydari and Kalyani Priyadarshan added their own statements — minimalist gowns, heritage-inspired jewellery, and a deliberate emphasis on Indian craftsmanship over Western designer labels.

For NRIs watching from New York, London, and Toronto, these red-carpet moments are more than celebrity gossip. They are proof of concept — evidence that Indian aesthetics can hold their own at the highest tier of global fashion without dilution or apology.

## Then the Trolls Arrived

If the sarees were the high point, the Alia Bhatt episode was the low. A brief clip from the red carpet, in which photographers appeared to overlook Bhatt momentarily, went viral — not because it was newsworthy, but because it gave the internet exactly what it craves: an opportunity to diminish an Indian woman succeeding abroad.

The clip was context-free and misleading. Bhatt, a L'Oréal Paris global ambassador making her second consecutive Cannes appearance, responded with characteristic poise: when one commenter wrote "No one noticed you," she replied, "Why pity, love? You noticed me."

But the damage was already spreading. Ameesha Patel posted a sharp rebuke on X, asking when Indians would learn to support their own. "Such a shame," she wrote, pointing out the disproportionate vitriol aimed at Indian celebrities compared to their Hollywood peers. Soni Razdan, Bhatt's mother, framed the trolling as a symptom of deeper societal malaise — "Social media doesn't create the ugliness, it just reveals it." Sonu Sood, Aly Goni, and Rahul Vaidya all weighed in with support.

## The Mirror and the Diaspora

This is the uncomfortable paradox that Cannes holds up every year. India sends its designers, actors, and producers to the world's most prestigious cultural gathering, and a significant chunk of the Indian internet responds with ridicule. The pattern is familiar to anyone in the diaspora: the same community that celebrates Sundar Pichai's Google keynote will mock an Indian actress for pausing on a carpet.

The roots run deeper than celebrity culture. For NRIs, the trolling of Bhatt touches a nerve because it mirrors the criticism many face from back home — the implication that international success is somehow unearned, or that visibility abroad is a form of showing off. The fact that much of the vitriol is gendered makes it worse.

## What Endures

A week from now, the trolling discourse will have evaporated. What will remain is the work: Manish Malhotra's gold-thread saree catching French sunlight, Amit Aggarwal's Ikat gown redefining what Indian textile innovation looks like at scale, and a generation of Indian designers using Cannes as a launchpad rather than a backdrop.

For the diaspora, the lesson is the same one it relearns every year: India's cultural exports are extraordinary. The conversation around them, less so. The sarees deserve better company than the trolls.
